evidence: Ter. Ad. 425: hoc salsum est; hoc adustum est
Hor. S. 2.8.68: nē pānis adustus … adpōnātur
terms.comment: What Syrus says, tasting at the stove; Horace’s host fears burnt bread. Adūrere is to scorch, adustus burnt (Lewis & Short, citing both passages). See “burn”.

terms.gloss: scorch, let catch on the bottom of the pot
evidence: Cato Agr. 107: commovētō, vidētō nē adūrās
Col. 12.42.2: sit puer, quī spathā ligneā vel harundine permisceat pōma, nē possint adūrī
terms.comment: The verb for food that catches and burns on the bottom of the pot, and so for “it’s sticking”: the cook stirs so that it does not. That it has stuck fast is adhaerēre, a plain description; see the examples and “adhere”.

phrases.latin: Hoc salsum est; hoc adustum est; hoc lautum est parum; illud rēctē: iterum sīc mementō.
phrases.english: This is too salty; this is burnt; this isn’t washed enough; that one’s right: remember to do it that way again.

phrases.latin: nē pānis adustus, nē male condītum jūs adpōnātur
phrases.english: in case the bread is served burnt, or the sauce badly seasoned
Stir it, and see that you don’t burn it.

phrases.latin: Vae, sartāginī adhaesit! Cūr nōn versāvistī?
phrases.english: Oh no, it’s stuck to the pan! Why didn’t you turn it?
Stir it, so it doesn’t catch.
It’s burning! Turn the heat down.

sources: Lewis & Short: aduro · Lewis & Short: adhaereo
